stimulus.title: Pendulum timing data
stimulus.text:
A student wants to determine the magnitude of the gravitational field g in the classroom using a small metal bob on a light string hung from a clamp. The student has a meterstick, a stopwatch and a protractor.

The student's data for five lengths are shown. Length ℓ is measured from the pivot to the center of the bob; each bob was released from rest at about 8°.

table.caption: Length and time for 10 complete oscillations

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure the student could use to collect data like these. Include what is measured, with which equipment, and one way to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubric.point: Measures the length ℓ from the pivot to the center of the bob with the meterstick, for several (at least 5) different lengths
Releases the bob from rest at a small angle (checked with the protractor) and times the oscillations with the stopwatch
accept: small angle so the motion is close to SHM

rubric.point: Reduces uncertainty: times many oscillations (e.g. 10) and divides, and/or repeats each length and averages

parts.sample: Hang the bob from the clamp and use the meterstick to measure ℓ from the pivot to the center of the bob. Pull the bob aside to about 8° (protractor) and release it from rest. Start the stopwatch as it passes the bottom and time 10 full oscillations; divide by 10 to get T. Repeat three times for each length and average. Do this for five lengths from 0.20 m to 1.00 m.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Indicate what quantities could be graphed to yield a straight line whose slope could be used to determine g. Explain how g is found from the slope.

rubric.point: Graphs T² (vertical) against ℓ (horizontal), or ℓ against T²
accept: T against √ℓ also earns the point

rubric.point: States the slope relation from T = 2π√(ℓ/g): slope = 4π²/g so g = 4π²/slope (or g = 4π² × slope for ℓ against T²)
accept: for T against √ℓ: slope = 2π/√g, so g = 4π²/slope²

parts.sample: Square T = 2π√(ℓ/g): T² = (4π²/g)ℓ. A graph of T² against ℓ is a straight line through the origin with slope 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/slope.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: On the grid, plot the data points for the quantities you indicated in part (b). Clearly label the axes with quantities and units, use a linear scale, and draw a best-fit line for the data.

rubric.point: Axes labeled with quantities and units (T² in s², ℓ in m) and a linear scale that uses most of the grid
accept: both label and unit on each axis

rubric.point: Points plotted correctly: T² = 0.81, 1.59, 2.43, 3.20, 4.04 s² at ℓ = 0.20 to 1.00 m
A single straight best-fit line through the data, close to the origin; not connect-the-dots
accept: roughly as many points above as below

parts.sample: Computed T = t/10, then T²: 0.20 m → 0.81 s²; 0.40 m → 1.59 s²; 0.60 m → 2.43 s²; 0.80 m → 3.20 s²; 1.00 m → 4.04 s². With T² on the vertical axis (0 to 4.5 s²) and ℓ on the horizontal axis (0 to 1.0 m), the points lie close to one straight line through about the origin; draw a single ruler line through them.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate an experimental value for g using the best-fit line.

rubric.point: Slope found from two well-separated points on the line (not data points unless on the line), about 4.0 s²/m
accept: slope between 3.8 and 4.2 s²/m, with units

rubric.point: g = 4π²/slope, about 9.8 m/s², consistent with the student's slope
accept: value between 9.4 and 10.4 m/s² with units

parts.sample: Two points on my line: (0.10 m, 0.40 s²) and (0.90 m, 3.63 s²). Slope = 3.23 s² / 0.80 m = 4.04 s²/m. g = 4π²/slope = 39.48 / 4.04 s²/m = 9.8 m/s².
